::: {.oneline}
Not a susceptibility and not a spectrum, but a number of counts at a detector,
already averaged over collection angle, spectral width and acquisition time,
with the whole apparatus folded in.
:::

## Short answer

The raw output of an optical experiment is a number of counts per second, as a
function of whatever was scanned. Turning this into something a theorist
recognizes means undoing a chain of steps, and information is lost at each of
them.

The detector collects over a finite range of angles, so that anything
anisotropic is already partly averaged. It has finite spectral resolution, so
that sharp features are broadened by the instrument as well as by the physics.
It integrates over an acquisition time far longer than any dynamics in the
sample, so that what is reported is a time average over many events. Its
efficiency depends on wavelength and must be calibrated out. Finally the sample
sits on a substrate, in a particular geometry, with a spot size averaging over
inhomogeneity, strain and defects.

None of this is sloppiness, but simply what measuring means. It does explain,
however, why a computed peak and a measured peak rarely line up on first
comparison, and why the honest question is usually not whether the theory is
right, but whether the two numbers are even the same quantity.

The practical consequence is that we should make the comparison as far down the
chain as possible. Computing a susceptibility and comparing it with a measured
transmission compares different objects. Propagating the susceptibility through
the real geometry, applying the instrument response, and comparing count rates
with count rates is indeed more work, and considerably more convincing.

## Why it works this way

Every measurement is an interaction between sample and apparatus, and the
apparatus leaves its fingerprints on the result. Recognizing which features
belong to the sample and which to the setup is therefore a large part of
experimental skill, and the main reason why a theorist and an experimentalist
arguing about a discrepancy should first agree on what each of them is plotting.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The algebra: the chain from theory to counts

Schematically, the measured signal is

$$
S(\omega_{\text{set}}) = \eta(\omega)
\int d\Omega \int d\omega\; R(\omega - \omega_{\text{set}})\,
I\!\left[\chi(\omega), \text{geometry}\right] ,
$$ {#eq-measurement-chain}

with $\eta$ the detector efficiency, $R$ the instrument response function, the
angular integral set by the collection optics, and $I$ the intensity obtained by
propagating the response through the sample structure. Comparisons made before
the last two steps compare different quantities.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The algebra: broadening that is not physical

A computed spectrum is usually plotted with an artificial Lorentzian width
$\eta$ introduced to make discrete transitions visible on a finite grid. This is
not a lifetime. Reporting a linewidth extracted from such a plot as a physical
decay rate is a common and avoidable error, since the physical width comes from
the imaginary part of the self-energy, or from an explicitly computed scattering
rate.
:::

## Common confusions

- **"The measured linewidth is the intrinsic lifetime."** It also contains the
  instrument resolution and the inhomogeneous broadening across the illuminated
  spot.
- **"Photoluminescence is absorption run backwards."** Emission takes place
  after relaxation, from a different population of states, and often from states
  that are dark in absorption.
- **"Disagreement in absolute intensity means the calculation is wrong."** It
  frequently means that the geometry, the substrate or the collection efficiency
  has not been accounted for.
